schoolReviews.review: My daughter was assaulted several times and Ada Givens Elementary School in Merced, CA swept our complaints under the rug. Teachers give low scores at the beginning to later give higher scores giving false impression ofacademic progress thanks to their teaching. Teachers did not treat my child fairly and theCalifornia Department of Education routinely dismiss our complaints. School Principal is rude. Students disrupt teacher talking in class, skip class and strain the patience of teachers with rampant absences costing the school Federal attendance funds and causing teacher burnout. Celebrations involve loud music speakers pointed towards performing students causing Tinnitus(damage to ear nerves). My child scored near perfect score in IQ tests and transferred to a better school.

My child is currently in the fourth grade and has been at the school for three years. While Merced itself is socioeconomically problematic and the backgrounds of some of the students must be challenging, I can’t help but be impressed by this school. The staff is friendly and helpful and the teachers are amazing. Our experience as parents of a child at Ada Givens has been excellent so far. My child has loved every teacher he’s had and feels safe, happy, and motivated to learn here.
This school gave my kid hotdog water for lunch.

I have two boys that were enrolled in this school after moving to our new house, I went into the office and enrolled both my boys age 5 and age 7 one in kinder and the other in 2nd grade. I walked them both to there classes this morning along with the secretary and we all had a talk about my 7 year old walking to my 5 year's class and waiting for there pick up I was also told how my children would not be allowed to leave that class until there ride picked them up, However when my sister arrived to pick them up at 2:20pm no one knew where my kids were, the school did not even notify of my kids being lost and my sister was by the office staff o well she called me and told me what was going on I called the school and they acted like no big deal!! I did notify the police thank GOD my kids were found after walking home alone at age 5 and 7 more than 6 blocks away from the school! This school is a joke if you want your kids to be safe then this school is not right for you!!!!!!!
I feel this school has a great staff and a great ASSETS program after school hours.

We have loved this school. Three of our children attend this school. The parent involvment is really poor though but that is no reflection on the school, more the parents lack of care for thier kids. The teachers have been fabulous, especially Mrs. Pino ion 2nd grade. The principal and office staff are great.

schoolReviews.review: I have 2 students here. The one senior and one freshman. I like that it is the type of school where most students know each other from their younger days and yet, they have been welcoming to students like mine, who are transplants. Parents seem to be engaged, FFA seems great and there are lots of programs, clubs and pathways for students to explore.

This is an amazing campus to work at. I feel supported by both administration and parents, which is not always the case at other schools. I have some of the best kids in the district in my classes and for the most part, they all work hard and do their best. This is a wonderful school!!!

schoolReviews.review: Exceptional education, caring staff, wonderful families! It is now a preschool-6th grade community. I wouldn't want my kids to attend any other school.
Art, music, strong moral values plus a common core curriculum that teaches students how to think is the amazing school that is St. Paul in Merced.

I am a doctor who wants the best possible education for her child. I have researched so many different schools and options in the area and St. Paul consistently came out as the best. We are religious but not Christian and had concerns about how our child would be accepted at a Christian school. We chose this school after looking at all of our options in Merced and are EXTREMELY happy with it! It seems to be the best academically in the area and I appreciate that the teachers and administrators at the school truly live out the Christian mission and demonstrate love and caring for the children and their education. We are so incredibly grateful to St. Paul and everything it does for the children. Our son has thrived there and learned so much in a short time. We can't wait to see what he's like after a few years there! Kudos, St. Paul!

Our eldest child just started preschool at Saint Paul's 4 months ago. I was easily impressed by the school. However, my wife is a public school teacher, and came in very critical of "private vs. public education". She to, loves it. Our daughter has learned so much more than we would have guessed in such a short time. She is amazing us daily with her new found knowledge. The staff is wonderful, the teachers are actually allowed (unlike public school) to have a caring and loving heart for the children. We will be keeping her here and our youngest will also be going as soon as he is old enough.

St. Paul Lutheran School in Merced is absolutely the best school in the area. We love the other families, the teachers, the staff, and the kids. Advanced academics enriched with a loving environment. Couldn't ask for more. We'll be staying throughout our son's elementary school years.

St. Paul is an outstanding school. They have interactive white boards, computers in each class and continually teach at a level that get kids going one year above their peers in other schools. Couldn't say enough great things about this school.

Wind Factor is a tool created by the nonprofit First Street. It uses the First Street National Wind Model, which forecasts how hurricanes and costs from resulting wind damages to structures will change over time due to climate change.

A property's Wind Factor indicates its likelihood to experience extreme winds over the next 30 years, from 1 (minimal) to 10 (extreme). Properties with higher Wind Factor scores are more likely to experience higher winds more frequently today and in the future.

entryPointDescription.value: Based on the likelihood and speed of hurricane, tornado, or severe storm winds reaching this property, it has minimal wind risk.

scoreDescription.value: This property's wind risk is not significantly changing over time.

entrypointGraphFlyout.value: This chart shows this property's likelihood of being in a tropical storm event with 3-second wind gusts exceeding 50 mph (39 mph for 1-minute sustained winds) over the next 30 years.

riskFactorHomeURLText.value: See all wind data on firststreet.org

expandableSummary.value: Estimated 18-26% chance of a flood reaching the building in the next 30 years

entryPointFlyout.value:
Flood Factor® is a tool created by the nonprofit First Street. It uses the First Street Flood Model, a nationwide, probabilistic flood model that shows a location’s risk of flooding from rain, rivers, tides, and storm surge. It builds off of decades of peer-reviewed research and forecasts how flood risks will change over time due to changes in the environment. Flood Factor is not intended to include all possible risks of flood.

A property's Flood Factor is an indicator of its comprehensive flood risk, ranging from 1 (minimal) to 10 (extreme). Properties with higher Flood Factors are more likely to have flooded in the past, and are more likely to flood in the future.

entryPointDescription.value: Based on this property’s projected likelihood and depth of flooding, it has moderate flood risk.

scoreDescription.value: This property's flood risk is decreasing over time.

entrypointGraphFlyout.value: Flood risk accumulates over time. Cumulative risk is calculated to the largest building or center of an empty lot. Raised or elevated buildings may not be as vulnerable as ground-level buildings or buildings with basements.

entrypointGraphDescription.value: This property has a 22% chance of flooding in the next 30 years.

riskFactorHomeURLText.value: See all flood data on firststreet.org

riskSpecificSubsectionFlyout.value:
The FEMA flood zone shown is the most probable estimated zone.

The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) is a government agency that maps flood zones in communities across the US, identifying areas of varying flood risk on Flood Insurance Rate Maps (FIRMs). FEMA creates FIRMs to inform flood insurance pricing in the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) and to guide floodplain management regulations for NFIP-participating communities.

riskSpecificSubsectionFlyout2.value: The FEMA flood zone shown is the most probable zone as estimated by MassiveCert, Inc.

riskSpecificSubsectionDescription.value: This property is estimated to be in FEMA Zone AO, which is designated as a high-risk flood area.

insuranceFlyout.value: To help you understand what it costs to protect this home with flood insurance we've partnered with Neptune Flood. Redfin may receive a commission if you purchase a policy through this link. There may be other flood insurance providers in your area.

insuranceDescription.value:
Based on your estimated FEMA zone, flood insurance is required to obtain a mortgage from a federally regulated or insured lender.

Flood insurance for this home ranges from $848 to $2087 per year, based on information from 6 providers.

expandableSummary.value: 9% chance of being in a wildfire in next 30 years

entryPointFlyout.value:
Fire Factor is a tool created by the nonprofit First Street. It uses the First Street National Wildfire Model's nationwide, behavioral wildfire model that shows a specific location's probabilistic risk of wildfire based on the vegetation, topography, and fire weather in the surrounding area. Fire Factor is not intended to include all possible risks of fire.

A property's Fire Factor indicates its cumulative wildfire risk, ranging from 1 (minimal) to 10 (extreme). Properties with higher Fire Factors are more likely to be in a wildfire in the future.

entryPointDescription.value: Based on this property's distance to wildfire risk areas and burnable vegetation, it has major wildfire risk.

scoreDescription.value: This property's fire risk is increasing as weather patterns change.

entrypointGraphFlyout.value: Wildfire risk accumulates over time, so a property with a 0.1% chance of wildfire this year would have at least a 3% chance of being affected by wildfire at least once within 30 years. Being affected by wildfire refers to any actively burning fuels coming into contact with the largest building on the property.

entrypointGraphDescription.value: Within the next 30 years, this property has a 9% cumulative chance of being in a wildfire.

FEMA creates FIRMs to inform flood insurance pricing in the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) and to guide floodplain management regulations for NFIP-participating communities.

riskSpecificSubsectionDescription.value: This property is located in a county with an average wildfire risk greater than 69.20% of counties in the United States.

insuranceFlyout.value: Most homeowners insurance typically includes fire coverage but in some areas, this will need to be purchased separately. Investing in fire insurance is one way to offset the cost of wildfire damage, and can help reduce your financial risk.

insuranceDescription.value: Fire insurance for this home ranges from $659 to $1223 per year, based on information from 7 providers.

expandableSummary.value: 7 days above 104° expected this year, 17 days in 30 years

entryPointFlyout.value:
Heat Factor is a tool created by the nonprofit First Street. Heat Factor™ uses the First Street Extreme Heat Model to determine property-specific heat risk across the United States. The model is a spatial temperature model that determines a specific location’s exposure to extreme heat events based on the surface temperature, topography, land cover, and humidity in the surrounding area.

A property's Heat Factor indicates its risk of extreme heat exposure over the next thirty years, ranging from 1 (minimal risk) to 10 (extreme risk). Heat Factors are based on the current average daily high temperature and humidity of a property’s specific location during the hottest month of the year, and considers how it’s expected to grow over the next 30 years.

entryPointDescription.value: Based on current and future temperature and humidity in the area and at this specific location, this property has severe heat risk.

scoreDescription.value: This property's heat risk is increasing as weather patterns change.

entrypointGraphFlyout.value: This chart shows the number of days exceeding what is considered a hot day at this property. This is defined by using the 98th percentile “feels like” temperature in this area, or the hottest 7 days in the 4km area surrounding this property for a given year and using the lowest “high” temperature from those 7 days as a base. A property may have more or less hot days than the surrounding area depending on its individual exposure to heat.

entrypointGraphDescription.value: A “hot day” in this area is considered to be any day with a “feels like” temperature of 104º. Over the next 30 years, this property is expected to see a 10% increase in the number of hot days per year.

riskFactorHomeURLText.value: See all heat data on firststreet.org

entryPointFlyout.value: A property's Air Factor indicates the number of poor air quality days it will experience over the next 30 years, from 1 (minimal) to 10 (extreme). Properties with higher Air Factor scores are more likely to experience poor air quality days today and in the future.

entryPointDescription.value: Based on the expected number of poor air quality days where the Air Quality Index (AQI) exceeds 100, this area has extreme air quality risk.

scoreDescription.value: This property's air risk is increasing as weather patterns change.

entrypointGraphTitle.value: Poor air quality days over time

entrypointGraphFlyout.value: This chart shows the change in the number of poor air quality days over time, where the Air Quality Index (AQI) exceeds 100. These are the expected number of poor air quality days in a bad year, which is defined as a year with higher than average wildfire activity. This increases the amount of particulate matter (PM2.5) in the air and therefore worsens air quality.

entrypointGraphDescription.value: Over the next 30 years, this area will experience a 5.3% increase in the number of poor air quality days, i.e. where the Air Quality Index (AQI) exceeds 100.
